discovery: Prediction and theory of kilonovae: neutron-star mergers as the cosmic site of r-process heavy-element nucleosynthesis, confirmed by GW170817

nominees.name: Li-Xin Li
nominees.affiliation: Kavli Institute for Astronomy and Astrophysics, Peking University, China

nominees.name: Brian D. Metzger
nominees.affiliation: Columbia University and Flatiron Institute, USA

subfield: Astrophysics / multi-messenger astronomy and nuclear astrophysics
motivation: Where were the heaviest elements, such as gold, platinum and the lanthanides, made? Lattimer (with Schramm) first proposed that decompressed neutron-star matter ejected in compact-binary mergers forges r-process nuclei. Li and Paczynski predicted that the radioactive decay of this ejecta powers a transient optical/infrared glow. Metzger and collaborators developed the self-consistent theory of these 'kilonovae', predicting their luminosity, timescale and, together with lanthanide opacities, their red colour. In August 2017 the gravitational-wave event GW170817, localized by LIGO-Virgo and followed by about seventy observatories, revealed exactly this signal: a rapidly evolving blue-to-red kilonova whose spectra showed the fingerprints of freshly synthesized heavy elements. These predictions guided the global follow-up campaign and turned a gravitational-wave detection into a laboratory for nucleosynthesis, dense-matter physics and cosmology. They answered a long-standing question about the origin of the elements and opened multi-messenger astronomy with gravitational waves.
